extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers learning category theory
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory-to-intermediate textbook exposition giving formal definitions, examples, and basic properties of categories, functors, natural transformations, and foundational set-theoretic devices (universes, small vs large).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A category consists of objects and arrows together with a composition operation on arrows that is associative and has identity arrows for each object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes an arrows-and-axioms viewpoint (rather than hom-sets). Equivalently, a category can be seen as a monoid for a suitable product. Examples and minimal categories (empty category, one-object category, small finite categories) illustrate the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty and finite example categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Small example categories: the empty category (no objects, no arrows); 1 (one object and its identity); 2 (two objects and one non-identity arrow); 3 (three objects with a specified pattern of non-identity arrows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show composition constraints and uniqueness of composition definitions in very small categories; they are illustrative rather than additional axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete category
rubrics_metrics.description: A category is discrete when every arrow is an identity; each set X corresponds to a discrete category with objects X and identity arrows x→x for each x∈X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrete categories are essentially equivalent to sets; the construction is 'just add identity arrows.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Monoid as a category with one object
rubrics_metrics.description: A monoid is exactly a category with one object: its arrows form a set M with associative binary operation and identity element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus hom(a,a) for an object a in any category is a monoid. This identifies algebraic monoids with one-object categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group as a one-object category with inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: A group is a category with one object in which every arrow has a two-sided inverse under composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group-theoretic axioms correspond exactly to category-theoretic invertibility in one-object categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix category Matr_K
rubrics_metrics.description: For a commutative ring K, Matr_K is the category whose objects are positive integers and whose arrows n→m are m×n matrices with entries in K, composition given by matrix multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows categories whose objects are 'sizes' and arrows are algebraic data (matrices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category of sets (Ens / Set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection V of sets, Ens_V is the category with objects X∈V and arrows all functions f:X→Y, with usual composition; Set denotes the category of all small sets (see universe discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names: Ens for category of sets within a specified collection V; Set reserved for small sets constructed via a chosen universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preorder as a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A preorder is a category P in which for any objects p,p' there is at most one arrow p→p'. This corresponds to a reflexive, transitive binary relation on the objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, any reflexive, transitive relation yields a preorder category; partial orders and linear orders are special cases. Composition and identities are uniquely determined by the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinals and Finord / simplicial category
rubrics_metrics.description: Each ordinal n is a linearly ordered set and hence a category (a preorder). The simplicial category Δ (denoted A in the text) has objects finite ordinals and arrows the order-preserving functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finord and related categories (Finord, Set_f) are important examples used later (e.g., Chapter VII). The category Finord has as arrows all functions between finite ordinals (essentially finite sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large categories and the universe device
rubrics_metrics.description: To form an actual category of all small sets (Set), assume a sufficiently large set U (a 'universe'); call elements of U 'small sets' and take Set to have objects the small sets and arrows the small functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device lets one avoid paradoxes while creating large categories. Details of the universe are given in the foundations section with explicit closure properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of standard (particular) categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard categories include Set (small sets), Set_* (pointed sets), Ens (sets within V), Cat (small categories, arrows = functors), Mon (small monoids), Grp, Ab, Rng, CRng, R-Mod, Mod-R, K-Mod, Top, Toph, Top_*, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are used as running examples; the text indicates they will be printed in boldface and that script capitals are commonly used to denote categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a functor
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor T:C→B assigns to each object c of C an object Tc of B and to each arrow f:c→c' an arrow Tf:Tc→Tc' in B, preserving identities and composition: T(g∘f)=Tg∘Tf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described in 'arrows-only' fashion: a function on arrows carrying identities to identities and composable pairs to composable pairs with preservation of composition. Example: power set functor P: Set→Set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of functors (homology, GL_n, forgetful functors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functors arise in topology (singular homology H_n: Top→Ab), algebra (GL_n: CRng→Grp), and via forgetful functors (e.g., U:Grp→Set) which 'forget' structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate covariant functors and mention contravariant behavior (later). Forgetful functors often are faithful but not full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and identity for functors; category of categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Functors compose: given S:B→A and T:C→B, their composite S∘T:C→A is a functor. The identity functor I_B:B→B acts as identity for composition. One can form categories whose objects are categories and arrows are functors (metacategory), and Cat for small categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition is associative; caution that the category of all categories (without size restriction) is problematic, hence Cat is category of small categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism of categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor T:C→B is an isomorphism if it is bijective on objects and arrows equivalently if there exists S:B→C with S∘T and T∘S equal to identity functors; then S is the two-sided inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isomorphism is a strict notion (bijective on both objects and arrows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Full functor
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor T:C→B is full when for every pair c,c' of objects in C and every arrow g:Tc→Tc' in B there exists an arrow f:c→c' in C with Tf=g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: on hom-sets the induced functions hom(c,c')→hom(Tc,Tc') are surjective. Composites of full functors are full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful functor (embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor T:C→B is faithful when for every pair of objects c,c' in C the induced map on hom-sets hom(c,c')→hom(Tc,Tc') is injective (i.e., T distinguishes parallel arrows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: cancellation on composition by T implies equality of original arrows. Composites of faithful functors are faithful. Example: U:Grp→Set is faithful but not full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully faithful functor
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor that is both full and faithful; equivalently the induced hom-functions are bijections for every pair of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully faithful need not be an isomorphism of categories if it fails to be essentially surjective (there may be objects of B not in the image of T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategory and full subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: A subcategory S of C is a collection of some objects and arrows of C closed under domains/codomains, identities, and composition; the inclusion map S→C is an inclusion functor which is automatically faithful. S is a full subcategory if the inclusion is full (i.e., contains all arrows between its objects that exist in C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full subcategory of C is determined just by its set of objects. Example: Set_f (finite sets) is a full subcategory of Set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a natural transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given functors S,T:C→B, a natural transformation η:S⇒T assigns to each object c∈C an arrow η_c: S c → T c in B such that for every arrow f:c→c' in C the naturality square commutes: T f ∘ η_c = η_{c'} ∘ S f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components η_c are called components; the arrows form a 'translation' between the pictures S and T. Arrows-only description: a function sending each arrow f to tf satisfying coherence equations (Exercise 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural isomorphism / natural equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural transformation whose each component η_c is invertible in B is a natural isomorphism (written η: S ≅ T); inverses of components assemble into the inverse natural transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural isomorphism is the notion of equality of functors up to coherent isomorphism; used to define equivalence of categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of natural transformations (determinant, projections, character duals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: determinant det_K: GL_n(K) → K* is a natural transformation between GL_n and (–)* functors on CRng; projections to factor-commutator groups give natural transformations on Grp; double character map γ: G → D(D G) is natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts are given: center Z(G) does not define a functor naturally; isomorphisms that depend on choices (e.g., identification of finite abelian group with its character group) are not natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of categories
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence between C and D is a pair of functors S:C→D, T:D→C together with natural isomorphisms I_C ≅ T∘S and I_D ≅ S∘T; this compares categories that are 'alike' though possibly of different sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence is weaker than isomorphism but the appropriate notion of 'same up to structure' in category theory; example given involving Finord and Set_f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertible arrow / isomorphism of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: An arrow e:a→b is invertible if there exists e':b→a with e'∘e=1_a and e∘e'=1_b; such e' is unique and denoted e^{-1}. Two objects a and b are isomorphic if there is such an invertible arrow between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isomorphism of objects is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monic (monomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arrow m:a→b is monic when for any parallel arrows f1,f2:d→a the equality m∘f1 = m∘f2 implies f1 = f2; i.e., m is left-cancellable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Set and Grp, monic arrows are precisely injections. If an arrow has a left inverse (a retraction) it is monic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epi (epimorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arrow e:a→b is epi when for any arrows g1,g2:b→c the equality g1∘e = g2∘e implies g1 = g2; i.e., e is right-cancellable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Set, epis are surjections. A right inverse (section) implies epi; the converse holds in Set but fails in Grp. Split epis/monics and idempotents splitting are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split monos, split epis, idempotents and splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: If g∘h = 1 then g is a split epi and h a split monic; an idempotent f:b→b (f∘f=f) is said to split when there exist arrows g,h with f = g∘h and h∘g = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions describe when certain canonical factorizations exist and relate to categorical decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal, initial, and null objects; zero arrows
rubrics_metrics.description: An object t is terminal if for every object a there is exactly one arrow a→t. An object s is initial if for every a there is exactly one arrow s→a. A null object z is both initial and terminal; with a null object there is a unique zero arrow a→z→b between any two objects, and composites with zero arrows are zero arrows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in Set the empty set is initial and any one-point set is terminal; in Grp the trivial group is both initial and terminal; Ab and R-Mod have null objects (zero groups/modules); Set_* has null object the one-point set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupoid and connected groupoid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A groupoid is a category in which every arrow is invertible. A connected groupoid is one with an arrow between any two objects; such a connected groupoid is determined up to isomorphism by a group (one of the hom(x,x)) and a set (the set of objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental groupoid π(X) of a topological space X is an example: objects are points, arrows homotopy classes of paths. hom_G(x,x) are groups and conjugation yields isomorphisms between isotropy groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational restriction: comprehension only inside a set U
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid paradoxes, comprehension is restricted: given a property φ(x) and a set U one allows the set {x | x∈U and φ(x)} but not arbitrary comprehension over all sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates introducing a universe U of 'small sets' closed under various operations so ordinary mathematics can be carried out within U while U and sets formed from U are used to build large categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and closure properties of a universe U
rubrics_metrics.description: A universe U is a set satisfying closure properties: (i) x∈U ⇒ x⊆U, (ii) if u,v∈U then {u,v}, (u,v), and u×v ∈ U, (iii) x∈U ⇒ P(x) ∈ U and U^x ∈ U, (iv) ω∈U (finite ordinals), (v) if f:a→b is surjective with a∈U and b⊆U then b∈U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These closure properties ensure standard set-theoretic operations applied to elements of U produce elements of U; condition (v) corresponds to Replacement. Working inside a chosen U yields the category Set of small sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms and Replacement axiom (foundational assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition assumes the standard ZF axioms (extensionality, null set, pair/set constructions, infinity, choice, regularity, replacement). Replacement: the image of a set under a functional property is a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacement implies the restricted comprehension used; combined with universe conditions, elements of U satisfy ZF axioms. Some authors instead use Gödel-Bernays with sets and classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes vs small sets and large categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A class is any subset C⊆U (so small sets are classes but some classes like U are not small sets). Proper classes are classes that are not small sets. Large categories have objects and arrows that are classes; some constructions (e.g., category Cis of all classes, Cat' of all large categories) exceed class-size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how to treat small sets, classes, and larger collections and why one universe suffices for many purposes; warns that Set and Grp are not small categories.
